ABSTRACT
Many road collisions originate from safety-critical information that
exists in the traffic environment but does not reach the driver in
time: a stationary truck beyond a curve, an oncoming vehicle
occluded by the vehicle being overtaken, or a cascade of successive
braking events. This work investigates whether vehicle-to-vehicle
(V2V) communication, combined with a lightweight neural network
executed on the vehicle’s embedded hardware, can provide timely
and actionable warnings in four such scenarios.
The scenarios were modelled in SUMO using the Veins and
OMNeT++ co-simulation framework. With cooperative warning
enabled, three scenarios that resulted in collisions in the baseline
configuration were completed without contact, while the fourth
maintained larger inter-vehicle gaps. A synthetic dataset of 10,000
samples was generated and used to train an 11–16–16–2 fully
connected network (498 parameters) that jointly predicts collision
risk and recommended speed, achieving test errors of 0.039 (risk)
and 0.134 m/s (speed). The trained model was exported as C code
and deployed on an ESP32, with a mean inference time of 57 µs
iv
and a maximum deviation of 3.3 × 10⁻⁶ from the reference
implementation across 1,215 inference requests. Two ESP32-S3
nodes now exchange vehicle state over ESP-NOW at 10 Hz.
In closed-loop braking tests, the proposed system reduced closing
speed at impact by roughly 93%, from 2.7 to 0.2 m/s, although a
collision was not entirely eliminated. This is attributed to the
independent estimation of risk and speed and to oscillation at close
range, both of which motivate a supervisory controller. Phase II will
add a supervisory controller, a custom PCB, a broadcast-beacon
link, and RC-vehicle validation.

CHAPTER 1
INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background and motivation
Many serious road collisions come down to a driver learning
about a hazard too late. The hazard is usually easy to understand once it
has been seen: a truck stopped just beyond a bend, an oncoming car
hidden behind the lorry that a driver is trying to overtake, a line of cars
braking one after another on an open road. In every one of these cases
the information already exists somewhere on the road. It just is not in the
line of sight of the vehicle that needs it.
Vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication is a way of passing
that information along. Each vehicle broadcasts its position, speed and
braking state, and nearby vehicles pick the message up directly, with no
cellular network in between. SAE J2735 defines the Basic Safety
Message used for this, while IEEE 802.11p and the IEEE 1609 family
cover the radio and networking layers (Kenney 2011). If a message
arrives while the hazard is still hidden, a following driver can gain
several seconds that a camera or radar could never give.
Receiving a message, though, does not tell the vehicle what to
do about it. It still has to turn the sender's state into a judgement of how
dangerous the situation is and how fast it should be going. That
judgement must be made on board, within a fraction of a control cycle,
and it must stay sensible when messages arrive late or not at all. Machine
learning suits the task, but most of the V2X learning work reviewed for
this project runs on servers or workstations. The question here was how
small the estimator could be made, and whether it could still be trusted
once it was moved onto a microcontroller.
The project therefore brings together three pieces: highway
scenarios simulated with SUMO and Veins, a compact neural network
that returns a collision risk and a recommended speed, and an ESP32
prototype in which two boards exchange vehicle state over ESP-NOW
and run the network locally. By the end of Phase I the network, with 498
parameters and about 2 KB of weights, ran on the ESP32 in roughly 57
µs per inference, and two ESP32 boards could exchange state and close a
simple speed-control loop.
1.2 Problem statement
A vehicle receives a state message from another vehicle about
ten times a second. It combines that message with its own speed, the gap
to the other vehicle and some measure of how reliable the link is. From
these eleven quantities it must estimate the probability that the situation
ends in contact, and advise a speed that avoids it. The estimate has to be
produced on the vehicle itself, so that no decision depends on a remote
server.
The information is incomplete for two reasons. One is
geometry: a bend, a hillside or another vehicle can hide the hazard from
the on-board sensors. The other is the radio link, where messages can be
delayed, dropped or relayed through several hops, so the sender's state is
already out of date when it is used. For this reason the model receives the
packet delivery ratio, the age of the last message and a hop count
alongside the kinematic quantities, and it is expected to grow more
cautious as the link gets worse.
Producing a number is only part of the job. The value must
mean the same thing in firmware as it did in training, it must arrive early
enough to be useful, and any speed command built from it must be one
that a real vehicle can follow. The oscillation at close range seen in the
closed-loop tests (Chapter 7) shows that a fast, numerically exact
inference is not enough by itself.

A note on terminology first. The first network output is called
model risk. Its training label is the fraction of 60 simulated roll-outs that
ended in contact, so the output estimates that fraction inside the bot-scale
simulator. It has not been compared with how often real vehicles collide,
so a dashboard reading of 80% should not be read as an 80% chance of a
real crash.
The prototype is a laboratory system. Speed, gap and
acceleration on the boards come from simple kinematics in the firmware,
and the boards pass these values to each other over ESP-NOW. GPS and
inertial sensing, motor control, public-road operation and compliance
with automotive safety standards were all outside Phase I.
One more point on scope concerns the radio link. In the
present prototype the two boards talk point to point, each configured with
the other's MAC address. This was intentional. The goal for Phase I was
only to show that two ESP32 boards can exchange vehicle state and act
on it. In the final system a vehicle will broadcast a beacon instead, and
any boards within range will pick it up and respond. Chapter 6 describes
the current arrangement and Chapter 8 the planned change.

CHAPTER 2
REVIEW OF LITERATURE
2.1 Overview
The literature relevant to this project falls into four groups:
learning-based collision prediction from V2X data, message
dissemination and traffic-level estimation over V2V links, the simulation
and communication tools used to study them, and machine learning on
small embedded devices. Four papers were read in full, and the rest are
placed using their abstracts and bibliographic records.
2.2 Collision prediction from V2X data
Ribeiro et al. (2023) predict collisions involving a
motorcyclist, whom they treat as a vulnerable road user. Communication
data are generated with the Veins framework, which couples SUMO with
the ns-3 network simulator, and stacked unidirectional LSTM layers are
trained on the resulting sequences. In the first scenario the model
predicted 96% of the collisions with an average prediction time of 4.53 s;
in the second it predicted 95% with 4.44 s. The cost was a high number
of false positives (78 and 68 events), and the correct-decision percentage
stayed at 41% and 43%. The authors conclude that the output is good
enough to warn a rider but not to trigger automatic emergency braking.
Two points from that study influenced this project. The false
positives are a reminder that a predictor with high recall needs a plan for
the times it is wrong, which is why minimum gaps and contact outcomes
are reported in simulation here, not just regression error. And an LSTM
that reads a time series is a heavier object than a feed-forward network
that reads a single state vector. The 4.5 s figure is also worth reading
carefully: it measures how far ahead of a collision the prediction was
made, not how long the computation took, so it cannot be set against the
microsecond inference times reported later.
Zou et al. (2023) consider an automated vehicle approaching a
pedestrian who is completely hidden by vehicles in the adjacent lane. A
baseline strategy is compared with one that uses V2V messages from the
neighbouring vehicles. Without V2V, the time to collision is close to
zero when the pedestrian is detected, and the vehicle brakes hard but still
hits the pedestrian. With V2V it can brake in proportion to the hazard,
the time to collision stays larger and the pedestrian crosses safely. The
experimental design, a baseline run and a V2V run from identical starting
conditions, is the one followed in Chapter 7.
Other recent work approaches the same family of problems
from different directions. Ben-Mosbah et al. (2024) study the electronic
emergency brake light application over 5G NR V2V, the same situation
as the braking-chain scenario here but with a cellular sidelink radio.
Farhat et al. (2024) propose a cooperative collision-avoidance system for
vehicular communication based on deep learning. Park et al. (2025)
combine C-V2X with camera-based object detection in a client–server
arrangement and report a mean broadcast latency of 9.24 ms for obstacle
information on a test track. None of these runs its model on a
microcontroller, which is the gap this project tries to fill.
2.3 Message dissemination and traffic estimation
Li et al. (2022) look at the load that safety messages place on
the network. Their end–edge–cloud architecture lets edge nodes predict
future vehicle trajectories and the density of vehicles along them. A
warning is then sent only to vehicles expected to pass through the
affected area, and the system switches between V2V and V2I delivery
depending on connectivity. On a real-world VANET mobility dataset it
outperformed schemes that ignore the predicted trajectory density. That
work is about who should receive a message, whereas this project is
about what the receiver does with it. The two fit together, since an
estimator can only act on state that is still fresh.
Wang et al. (2019) detect road congestion with V2V
messages. A fuzzy controller built on vehicle speed and traffic density
grades the local congestion level, neighbouring vehicles are asked for
theirs, and a hypothesis test over a large sub-sample gives a regional
estimate. In simulation the detection accuracy was 5.5% higher than a
geomagnetic-coil method and 7.5% higher than the CoTEC method,
while the V2V network overhead was 90.8% lower than CoTEC.
Congestion and imminent collision are different targets, since a slow,
dense queue need not contain any conflict and a collision can arise on an
empty road. What carries over from this paper is the idea of computing a
compact local estimate on each vehicle and exchanging only what
neighbours need.
Zardosht et al. (2017) use V2V messages for another purpose,
deciding when a driver should be rerouted after an accident. Their
module estimates the accident duration, takes traffic congestion and the
type of area into account, and was evaluated in city and highway
simulations with different proportions of V2V-equipped vehicles. It
reduced waiting and travel times. The time scale is minutes rather than
seconds, so it does not compete with this work, but it shows the same
pattern: a small decision module on each vehicle, fed by neighbour data.
2.4 Simulation, communication and embedded tools
The simulation side of the project rests on a well-established
tool chain. SUMO is an open-source microscopic traffic simulator in
which each vehicle follows a car-following model on a defined road
network (Lopez et al. 2018). Its TraCI interface lets an external program
read vehicle state and issue commands at every simulation step (Wegener
et al. 2008), which is how the four scenario controllers are written.
OMNeT++ is a discrete-event network simulator (Varga and Hornig
2008), and Veins couples it to SUMO so that vehicle motion and
wireless events influence each other (Sommer et al. 2011).
For the communication layer the project borrows ideas from
the U.S. DSRC family. IEEE 802.11p provides the radio, IEEE 1609 the
networking services, and SAE J2735 and J2945/1 define the message set
and its performance requirements (Kenney 2011). The prototype does not
implement these stacks. It uses ESP-NOW, a connectionless protocol
from Espressif that sends short frames directly between ESP32 boards
without an access point (Espressif Systems n.d.). The choice was a
practical one, not a standards-based one, and Chapter 3 explains how
closely the prototype follows the standards.
On the embedded side, TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers
shows that neural-network inference can fit in tens of kilobytes (David et
al. 2021), and Pohuliai et al. (2026) compare several TinyML models for
sensor classification on the ESP32. No runtime library was used here. A
network with two hidden layers of this size is simple enough to export as
plain C arrays and a few loops, which keeps the firmware transparent and
makes it easy to check against the training framework.

The comparison is qualitative on purpose. The studies differ

and an exact copy of that network runs on a microcontroller, where its
timing and its numerical agreement with the training framework are
measured.
CHAPTER 3
SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
3.1 Overall architecture
The system has two layers built around one idea. The first is a
simulation layer, in which cars drive through four hazardous situations
on a highway and exchange messages. The second is a hardware layer at
the scale of small bots, in which two ESP32 boards run the same kind of
estimator. Figure 3.1 shows how the stages connect.
Figure 3.1 Conceptual simulation and learning architecture
SUMO moves the vehicles, and TraCI lets a Python controller
read their state and give commands at every 0.1 s step. OMNeT++
models the wireless side and Veins couples the two simulators. The
scenario runs and the Monte-Carlo generator described in Chapter 4
produce labelled data, which are cleaned and normalised before training.
The trained network is exported as a C header, flashed onto an ESP32
and exercised from a laptop dashboard or from a second board. The
sensing and vehicle stages of the planned RC platform come after the
blocks in the figure and are not part of Phase I.
3.2 Development workflow
Figure 3.2 Development workflow from simulation to hardware
Figure 3.2 puts evaluation before deployment, and
deployment before V2V integration and system testing. The project
followed the same order. The network was first judged on held-out data,
then copied into C and compared with the training framework, and only
then connected to a second board. Every step ends in a measurable
check: test error, maximum difference between outputs, inference time
and, for the closed-loop tests, minimum gap.
3.3 Highway scale and bot scale
The project works at two scales, and it helps to keep them
apart. The SUMO scenarios use highway-scale numbers: vehicles
travelling at 14 to 30 m/s, gaps of hundreds of metres and radio ranges of
300 to 500 m. The dataset and the ESP32 boards use bot-scale numbers
chosen for the small RC vehicles of Phase II: speeds of at most 5 m/s,
gaps below 25 m and a time-of-flight sensor range of 4 m. The network
is trained on bot-scale data only. The highway runs show what
cooperative warning achieves in realistic conditions, while the bot-scale
model is the one that actually runs on the board.
Braking differs as well: 6 to 9 m/s² in the highway runs,
against 1.5 to 3.0 m/s² for the bots. Carrying the highway risk formula
over to the bots would have given thresholds that do not match their
stopping ability, which is why a separate dataset was generated.
3.4 Vehicle information and model inputs
Position, speed, acceleration, heading and braking state are
what a vehicle needs to share. The network, however, does not take raw

4.7 Bot-scale dataset
The training data come from a separate generator at bot scale,
which simulates the four situations with small kinematic roll-outs. Its
design assumptions were fixed by the team and not measured on
hardware: vehicle lengths of 0.22 m (car) and 0.40 m (truck), a standstill
gap of 0.10 m, braking of 1.5 to 3.0 m/s² (2.0 m/s² when comfortable), an
actuation lag of 60 to 120 ms, a 100 ms beacon interval, a ToF sensor
with 4.0 m range and 40 ms read lag, and roll-outs with a 30 ms step
over a 3.6 s horizon.
For each sampled state the generator runs 60 randomised roll-
outs, varying quantities such as actuation lag and braking capability, and
counts how many end in contact. The risk label is that fraction:
𝑦 = 1 ∑60 1[contact in roll−out i] (4.4)
The recommended-speed label is the highest speed from
which the vehicle can still recover, given the information delay. Because
the labels are Monte-Carlo estimates, they carry sampling noise of their
own. With n = 60 roll-outs, the standard deviation of a label with true
value p is √(p(1 − p)/60), and averaging this over the test labels gives a
noise floor of 0.016. A risk error of 0.04 is therefore within a factor of
about 2.5 of the best any model could do on this data, and pushing it
lower would only mean fitting the noise.
The dataset has 10,000 rows, 2,500 for each scenario. It was
divided at random into 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test,
giving 6,982, 1,455 and 1,563 rows, and the test partition holds 380, 379,
387 and 417 rows for Scenarios 1 to 4. The split is made row by row and
not by roll-out or scenario run, so rows that are close neighbours in state
space can end up on both sides of it. The test error therefore estimates
how well the model interpolates within the sampled state space, and
nothing is claimed about states outside it.
Across the whole dataset the mean risk label is 0.41, and
39.7% of rows have a label above 0.5, so the training data are not
dominated by safe states. Scenario 4 has the highest mean risk (0.54) and
Scenario 3 the lowest (0.26). Of all rows, 67.8% are flagged as occluded
and 59.9% have a single hop. Appendix 1 lists the columns and their
ranges.

6.3 Link-quality inputs
Three of the model inputs describe the link, and the firmware
derives them from the packets themselves. The packet delivery ratio is
the number of packets received divided by the number expected, where
the expected count grows by the jump in sequence number each time a
packet arrives. Message age is the time since the last packet was
received. Hop count is read from the packet and is always 1 in the two-
board set-up. If nothing has been heard for 2 s, the bot treats the other as
silent and substitutes a zero speed, zero acceleration, an age of 250 ms
and a single hop.
These definitions are adequate for a first demonstration, but
they differ from the training data in three ways that will matter in Phase
II. First, the firmware PDR is cumulative since start-up, whereas the
dataset used a sliding window, so one early loss lowers it for a long time.
Second, message age is measured from reception and not from the
sender's timestamp, so it leaves out the time the packet spent in transit.
Third, a bot is considered alive during the first 2 s after boot even though
no packet has been received, so for that interval the model is fed
placeholder values for the other vehicle.
The occlusion flag is a heuristic. It is set when the other bot is
moving faster than 0.3 m/s and the gap is more than 4.5 m. The ToF
sensor assumed in the dataset reaches 4.0 m, so a gap beyond 4.5 m
means that the sensor could not have seen the other vehicle while the
V2V link could. In the present tests the gap is itself simulated, so the flag
shows how the input would be set and does not represent a real sensing
event.
6.4 From point-to-point exchange to a broadcast beacon
Pairing two boards by MAC address was a conscious
simplification. The goal at the end of Phase I was to show that two
ESP32 boards could exchange vehicle state over ESP-NOW and use it in
the model, and that goal was met: both bots ran the loop for the full
duration of the tests and responded to each other's state.
A road is not a pair of vehicles, however, and the planned
arrangement is different. Each vehicle will broadcast a beacon, and any
vehicles within range will receive it and respond. ESP-NOW supports a
broadcast address, so the radio itself needs no change, but the firmware
will have to be reorganised around it. It will need a table of nearby
senders keyed by identity, with PDR and message age kept separately for
each; a rule for choosing which neighbour to treat as the conflict vehicle;
and filtering by signal strength or distance, so that distant vehicles do not
clutter the table. These points are listed as Phase II work in Chapter 8.

7.8 Dynamic operation and timing
A 60 s dynamic-drive run produced 600 requests, with a mean
inference time of 57.2 µs and a maximum of 61 µs. The speed trace in
the closed-loop braking figure shows repeated fluctuations once the
vehicles are close. The controller internals needed to explain this were
not logged. The advised speed depends on a noisy-looking function of
gap and closing speed, and a controller that follows it with a fixed gain
can end up chasing it. This is a hypothesis, not a result.
The dashboard example reports 248 µs for inference and 31.8
ms for the round trip, and the 248 µs is higher than the serial figures. The
measurement boundaries differ, and the dashboard figure comes from a
single request with Wi-Fi traffic active on the board, so the larger
number may include cache and radio effects. This has not been
investigated further, and the two sets of values should not be compared
directly.
7.9 Interpretation
Three findings stand out. First, the model is small and fast:
498 parameters, about 2 KB, and roughly 57 µs per inference, which is a
tiny share of a 100 ms cycle. Second, the board reproduces the reference
network to about 3 × 10−6, so the deployed model is the trained model.
Third, in the sweeps the outputs move in the right direction for both gap
and link quality.
Against that, the closed-loop braking test shows that a fast and
accurate estimator is not yet a safe controller. The risk was low while the
ego vehicle accelerated, contact still occurred, and the speed oscillated at
close range. The dashboard example showed the same problem in a static
form, with a risk of 64.7% and an advised speed above the current one.
These are read as consequences of using two independent heads without
a rule that links them, a point taken up in the next chapter.
The evidence has limits. The risk label comes from a
simulation with assumed parameters, the held-out error is measured on
randomly split rows from the same generator, and the highway runs use a
scripted baseline driver. None of it is a measurement on real vehicles.
CHAPTER 8
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
8.1 Engineering significance and limitations
The project joins a compact model to an embedded
cooperative prototype and checks it at each junction. In simulation,
cooperative warning changed three of the four outcomes from contact to
no contact and widened the margin in the fourth. On the board, the
network runs in under a tenth of a millisecond and matches its training-
framework reference to about 3 × 10−6. The rest of the chain, from
sensing to actuation, has not been profiled.
The sweeps are useful checks of behaviour. A wider gap
lowers the risk and raises the advised speed, and worse link quality
makes the outputs more cautious. They cover only the chosen input
conditions, however, and do not establish behaviour over every
combination of inputs the network may meet.
The control side needs work. The braking comparison still
ends in contact, the speed oscillates at close range, and the dashboard
example shows the two outputs disagreeing. One contributor in the two-
board firmware may be the rate limit: a speed change of at most 0.08 m/s
per 100 ms tick allows a deceleration of only 0.8 m/s², while the dataset
assumes braking of 1.5 to 3.0 m/s². A controller that cannot brake as hard
as the labels assume will under-react to a high risk. This is an
observation from the code and has not yet been tested.
The prototype does not establish GPS or IMU accuracy, motor
response, radio performance on moving vehicles, or the transfer of
highway-scale behaviour to RC-scale motion. Safer roads remain the
intended application and not something this study measured.
8.2 Proposed supervisory controller
A supervisory layer between the model and the actuator is the
most direct response to these findings. It would check the learned advice
against simple physical and link-quality rules before the vehicle acts on
it. This layer has not been implemented.
The first rule concerns stale or missing information. The
present firmware proceeds without a first beacon, and for the first 2 s
after start-up it feeds placeholder values to the model. A supervisor
should define a safe state for that situation, such as a speed cap until a
valid packet arrives, and a message age beyond which the other vehicle
is treated as unknown. The age limit should come from vehicle dynamics
and be tested.
The second rule links the two outputs: if the risk exceeds a
threshold, the commanded speed should not exceed the current speed,
whatever the second head says. The third is a limit on acceleration while
a hazard is flagged, and the fourth a rate limit that matches the vehicle's
real braking capability. Smoothing or hysteresis on the advice could be
added to reduce oscillation, though each adds delay and so has to be tried
against minimum gap and stopping time.
To judge any of this, the existing controller stays as the
baseline, and the experiment is repeated from the same initial conditions,
communication trace and model weights. Only then can a change in
outcome be attributed to the new policy, and no improvement is claimed
until that has been done.

8.4 Conclusion
This work built a complete, if small, chain for cooperative
collision estimation. Four highway situations were modelled in SUMO
with Veins and OMNeT++, and in three of them the baseline driver
collided while the driver with V2V information did not. A bot-scale
dataset of 10,000 rows was generated, and an 11–16–16–2 network with
498 parameters was trained on it, reaching test errors of 0.039 for risk
and 0.134 m/s for speed.
The network was exported as C code and run on an ESP32 at
about 57 µs per inference, with a worst-case difference of 3.30 × 10−6
from its reference over 1,215 requests and no communication errors.
Two boards exchanged state over ESP-NOW at 10 Hz and adjusted their
speeds, and a laptop dashboard exercised the model over Wi-Fi.
The braking tests set the limit on what can be concluded.
Closing speed at contact dropped from 2.7 to 0.2 m/s, but contact still
occurred, and earlier than in the open-loop run. Collision avoidance has
therefore not been shown, and the independent outputs and the close-
range oscillation are the first control issues for Phase II. The next steps
are the broadcast beacon, a supervisory controller, and measurements on
an RC platform whose speed, gap and radio performance are recorded
independently.
